strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: few-shot adaptation of large multimodal models, where in-context learning is often unstable for smaller LMMs.

The proposed MAPD framework is clearly described and combines first-order MAML with soft prompt distillation and an attention-mapper, yielding a parameter-efficient adaptation method (≈24M trainable parameters).

The evaluation covers four VL-ICL Bench tasks with multiple baselines, shot settings, and test-time adaptation strategies, and the results generally show MAPD outperforming comparable prompt-distillation approaches under finetuning-based adaptation.

The paper includes useful ablation-style comparisons (Multi-Task, In-Context, Model-Avg, NoMeta-task), robustness tests under image perturbations, and an analysis of scaling with more shots and prompt tokens.
Limitations, broader impact, and computational overhead are discussed, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core components—MAML-based prompt tuning, attention-mapper projection, and soft prompts for VLMs—are adapted from prior work, and the paper does not convincingly establish a fundamental new capability beyond scaling/application to LMMs.

The attention-mapper is not isolated in an ablation: there is no comparison against the original LLaVA MLP projector under the same meta-learning/prompt-distillation setup, so the benefit of the proposed mapper itself remains unclear.
The evaluation is narrow: only four single-image tasks from VL-ICL Bench are used, with relatively small test sets and no multi-image or more complex reasoning tasks.

Baselines are limited: there is no comparison to standard prompt tuning, prefix tuning, LoRA, adapters, or improved ICL strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought, task instructions), making it difficult to position the method against the broader parameter-efficient adaptation literature.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported, and the observed improvements over the strongest baseline (Multi-Task^PD) are often modest; statistical significance is therefore unclear.

The claim of ‘strictly monotonic improvements’ is not fully supported at larger shot counts (e.g., TextOCR results plateau at 32–64 shots), and the ‘first exploration’ claim is somewhat overstated given closely related prior work.
The comparison to LLaVA-OneVision-72B is not apples-to-apples, since it compares ICL at 72B scale against MAPD with test-time finetuning, while using different training data and architectures.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or model release is linked, and key architectural details (e.g., attention-mapper dimensions, how prompt tokens are projected to the LLM embedding space, whether inner-loop updates include both θ and P) are ambiguous.
The test-time finetuning requirement is computationally expensive (~5× ICL), which limits practical deployment; this is acknowledged but not mitigated.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: few-shot adaptation of large multimodal models without expensive full-model finetuning.

Combines meta-learning (first-order MAML) with prompt distillation and an attention-mapper, and provides a reasonably detailed implementation appendix with data mixture, hyperparameters, and training setup.
Evaluates on several VL-ICL tasks and includes robustness tests against image perturbations, showing MAPD+FT is comparatively robust in those settings.
Parameter-efficient design trains only about 24M parameters and uses Qwen2.5-7B, which is practically appealing compared to full LMM finetuning.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The paper combines existing components: first-order MAML, prompt tuning/soft prompts, and an attention-mapper adapted from Najdenkoska et al. (2023). The extension to LMMs with Qwen2.5 is mostly an engineering change, and the claimed 'first exploration' is overstated given prior meta-learning and prompt-distillation work for vision-language models.

Evaluation is insufficient for a top-tier venue. Only four narrow single-image tasks are used, several with very small test sets (e.g., Operator Induction has 60 test examples). No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and many improvements over the strongest FT baseline are only 1-3%, which may be noise.

Missing key baselines. There is no comparison to standard prompt-tuning/PEFT methods such as Lester et al. (2021), prefix tuning, P-tuning, or LoRA, despite the paper claiming to compare with 'related prompt-tuning approaches.' There is also no apples-to-apples LLaVA-v1.5 baseline using the same Qwen2.5 LLM and the original MLP projector, so gains cannot be attributed to MAPD or the attention-mapper.

Confounded architecture changes. The method replaces both LLaVA v1.5's LLM (Vicuna to Qwen2.5) and its MLP projection (with an attention-mapper), but does not isolate the effect of each change. Improvements may come from the stronger LLM rather than from meta-learned prompt distillation.

The main claim that MAPD 'outperforms ICL' is not supported by the ICL results. MAPD with ICL adaptation is substantially worse than In-Context PD on Operator Induction, CLEVR, and TextOCR. MAPD's strong numbers require test-time finetuning with up to 30 gradient steps, which is not an in-context learning alternative and incurs roughly 5x more test-time compute.

Technical details are inconsistent and under-specified. Equation (1) uses sigma(QK^T)*V and the text says softmax; there is no scaling factor; layer norm, residual connections, output projection, and exact integration with LLaVA/Qwen2.5 are not fully described. The claim that soft prompts are 'distilled' from image features is not mechanistically demonstrated.

The central hypothesis—that smaller LMMs are overwhelmed by irrelevant image embeddings—is not directly tested. There is no probing, attention analysis, or information-theoretic measurement showing that MAPD removes task-irrelevant visual information.

The evaluation protocol is transductive and not compute-matched with ICL. Test-time adaptation finetunes on the support set of the same task and selects K using a validation loss, while ICL is compared without gradient updates. This makes the comparison against ICL misleading.

Scope and significance are limited. Tasks are mostly synthetic classification, simple arithmetic, counting, and OCR, rather than broad VQA. The model does not consistently beat LLaVA-OneVision on most tasks, despite the 'state-of-the-art' framing in the appendix.

Reproducibility is incomplete. No code or model release is linked in the main text, and several baseline details and prompt formats are only partially provided. The paper also contains minor typos and notation errors (e.g., D^{quoy}, inconsistent use of sigma/softmax), which reduces confidence in the rigor of the implementation.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: in-context learning in smaller LMMs is often inconsistent and does not improve monotonically with more shots.
Proposes a parameter-efficient approach (only ~24M trainable parameters) by combining soft prompts, an attention-mapper, and first-order MAML within LLaVA v1.5.
Provides a clear training pipeline with two stages, meta-task construction, inner/outer loop optimization, and a pseudo-algorithm.
Evaluates on four VL-ICL Bench tasks with multiple shot settings and compares against several prompt-distillation variants.
Includes useful ablations on prompt length, task induction subtasks, shot-selection strategies, and robustness to image perturbations.
Reports implementation details including data mixture, hyperparameters, model configuration, and training time, which helps reproducibility.
Results generally show MAPD with test-time finetuning outperforms ICL and the proposed baselines on the evaluated tasks, and exhibits more monotonic scaling with shots.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: it largely combines existing ideas such as soft prompt tuning, first-order MAML, and an attention-mapper inspired by prior work, applied to LLaVA/Qwen.
Missing important baselines: no comparison to standard prompt-tuning methods, LoRA/adapters, visual prompt tuning, full fine-tuning, or prior meta-prompt methods under the same base LMM.
The term 'distillation' is used loosely; the training objective is standard answer likelihood, with no explicit distillation loss between image features and prompts.
Evaluation scope is narrow: only four single-image VQA tasks from VL-ICL Bench, with relatively simple reasoning and no multi-image or broader multimodal benchmarks.
Main results omit 0-shot comparisons and do not report variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, making it hard to judge significance of the often small gains.
SOTA/outperformance claims are not fully supported: Table 9 shows LLaVA-OneVision-72B ICL outperforms MAPD on Operator Induction, CLEVR, and TextOCR, with MAPD only best on Open-MI.
Test-time finetuning requires up to 30 gradient steps and roughly 5x more computation than ICL, limiting practical applicability.
Changing the base LLM to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct confounds the contribution: gains may partly reflect the stronger LLM rather than the proposed prompt-distillation method.

Some methodological details remain unclear: attention-mapper architecture, masking/normalization, how prompt tokens are distilled from visual features, and why attention outputs are treated as soft prompts.
Robustness gains are modest, and the paper does not deeply analyze failure cases beyond a few qualitative examples.

strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant problem: few-shot adaptation of LMMs where ICL can degrade as shots increase.
Proposes a technically plausible approach (MAPD) combining meta-learning with prompt distillation and a multi-head attention mapper, trained parameter-efficiently (~24M parameters).

Provides extensive evaluation on VL-ICL Bench with multiple baselines (ICL, Multi-Task, In-Context, Model-Avg, NoMeta, LoRA) and ablations across architectures, prompt lengths, robustness, and attention entropy.
Main results show consistent improvements with test-time finetuning adaptation over ICL and PEFT baselines, with non-overlapping confidence intervals in several key comparisons.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameters, data mixture, meta-task creation, and training procedures in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the work combines existing ideas (first-order MAML, prompt tuning, attention-based projection) and extends prior meta-learning/prompt-tuning approaches to LMMs, making the core contribution largely empirical.

Evaluation is limited to four single-image tasks from a single benchmark (VL-ICL); broader VQA tasks, multi-image settings, and more diverse reasoning benchmarks are not covered, which limits claims of general cross-task generalization.

The method relies on test-time gradient adaptation (K≤30 steps), making it more computationally expensive than training-free ICL; although FLOPs-matched analysis is provided, practical efficiency and latency concerns remain.

The abstract's reported 21.2% improvement over ICL is not straightforwardly reproduced from the main tables; compared with the strongest ICL baseline (In-ContextPD), average gains are closer to ~16% across the four tasks.

In several ICL-adaptation settings, MAPD underperforms simpler baselines (e.g., Operator Induction: 9.6 vs. 12.1 for NoMeta-task), indicating that its benefits depend heavily on the test-time finetuning procedure.

Comparisons with publicly available LMMs are not apples-to-apples because the custom base LMM is trained on a different data mixture and architecture; the strongest evidence is within the custom base model only.
No code or pretrained model release is mentioned, which slightly weakens reproducibility despite detailed training details.

strengths: Tackles an important problem: few-shot VQA adaptation for LMMs, where ICL performance often fails to improve in low-data regimes.
Proposes a parameter-efficient approach (24M trainable parameters) combining an attention-mapper, soft prompts, and first-order MAML, with detailed implementation and training details.
Provides extensive experiments on VL-ICL Bench, multiple LMM architectures (Qwen2.5, Vicuna, SigLIP), ablations on projection layer designs, prompt length, image perturbations, and test-time compute.
Shows MAPD + FT can improve over ICL and LoRA in several settings, with monotonic gains as shots increase for some tasks.
Includes useful appendix material: finetuning data mixture, meta-task construction, hyperparameters, qualitative examples, and attention analysis.
weaknesses: Serious evaluation flaw: uses 10% of each test task's training split as a validation set for per-task hyperparameter and early-stopping selection, giving access to additional labeled data beyond the few-shot support set. This violates few-shot assumptions and likely inflates results.

Misleading comparisons and claims: the abstract's 'outperforming ICL by 21.2%' is not well-supported; MAPD under ICL adaptation is often worse than In-ContextPD; gains over ICL are confounded by comparing fine-tuning to no fine-tuning; the 7.7% gain is largely versus LoRA, while meta-learning over multi-task prompt distillation is only ~2.7%.

Limited novelty: the method combines existing components (MAML, prompt tuning, attention-based projection) with an incremental extension to LMMs; no fundamentally new technique or insight is introduced.

Central hypothesis not directly tested: the T2T vs I2T comparison does not control for task difficulty and does not prove that image embeddings overwhelm the LMM; no controlled experiment isolates the proposed interference effect.
Unfair or confounded comparisons: the base LMM uses a stronger Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct LLM and a modified architecture, so comparisons to LLaVA v1.5/OneVision and public LMMs are not apples-to-apples.

Results are not state-of-the-art: MAPD underperforms Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct FT on Open-MI, OP_IND, and TextOCR; it is only competitive on Open-MI and CLEVR, so broad superiority over existing methods is not demonstrated.
Missing baselines: no comparison to other meta-learning algorithms, other PEFT methods such as adapters or prefix tuning, or standard prompt tuning without meta-tasks under the same architecture.
Clarity and formatting issues: numerous typos ('optmization', 'Stricly', 'Psuedo', 'Cauldrion'), corrupted references with repeated/incorrect author names, and inconsistent table formatting.
Reproducibility concerns: no code release, no multiple training seeds, only binomial confidence intervals, and per-task validation makes exact replication difficult.
Narrow scope: evaluation is limited to four single-image tasks from VL-ICL; multi-image and many other reasoning tasks are excluded, limiting claims of cross-task generalization.

Attention entropy analysis is unconvincing: normalized entropy is not directly comparable across different numbers of prompts, and lower entropy may indicate more focused attention rather than failure.
Overclaims that the attention-mapper can be integrated into 'any LMM architecture' without testing integration into architectures such as LLaVA-OneVision or Qwen-VL.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: few-shot adaptation of large multimodal models for VQA, with a clear motivation based on the observed non-monotonic behavior of ICL in smaller LMMs.
Proposes a technically plausible and parameter-efficient approach (MAPD) that combines meta-learning, soft prompt distillation, and an attention-mapper module, training only about 24M parameters.

Provides extensive experiments on the VL-ICL Bench across four tasks, multiple prompt-distillation baselines, LoRA configurations, and several LMM architectures, showing consistent gains for test-time fine-tuning adaptation.

The attention-mapper is modular and can be integrated into LMM projection layers, and the paper includes useful ablations on projection-layer design, prompt length, task subtasks, robustness to image perturbations, and attention entropy.

The appendix is detailed, with meta-task construction, hyperparameter searches, qualitative examples, and additional scaling and compute analyses, improving reproducibility relative to many comparable papers.

The empirical results, especially on Open-MI and Operator Induction under test-time adaptation, support the claim that meta-learned prompt distillation can improve few-shot VQA over standard ICL and several PEFT baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method largely combines existing ingredients—prompt tuning, attention-based projection, first-order MAML, and LLaVA-style training—rather than introducing a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

Evaluation is narrow: only four single-image tasks from one benchmark (VL-ICL) are used, and some test sets are very small (e.g., Operator Induction has 60 query examples), which limits the strength and generality of the conclusions.

The headline comparison to ICL is not fully apples-to-apples: MAPD requires up to 30 test-time gradient steps, while ICL is training-free. The main text reports gains without jointly controlling for test-time compute, and the method’s own ICL adaptation is worse than In-ContextPD on three of four tasks.

Several gains are modest: against the strongest internal baseline (Multi-TaskPD), MAPD improves by only about 1.5–3.5 absolute points on CLEVR, TextOCR, and Operator Induction, with larger gains mainly on Open-MI.

No comparison is made to stronger external few-shot or meta-learning methods beyond LoRA and internal prompt-distillation variants; the paper also does not evaluate on standard real-world VQA datasets such as VQAv2, OKVQA, or TextVQA despite using them for training.

The central hypothesis—that LMMs are overwhelmed by irrelevant image embeddings and that the attention-mapper distills task-relevant visual features—is only indirectly supported by performance numbers; the attention-entropy analysis is post hoc and does not conclusively establish the claimed mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, some architectural details (e.g., how the attention-mapper output is projected to the LLM hidden dimension) are not fully specified in the main text, and the inner-loop step count differs between the main equations and appendix.
